trial_name: DESTINY II — Decompressive Hemicraniectomy in Older Patients with Malignant MCA Infarction (2014)
citation: Jüttler E, Unterberg A, Woitzik J, et al. Hemicraniectomy in older patients with extensive middle-cerebral-artery stroke. N Engl J Med. 2014;370(12):1091-1100.
trial_type: Randomised, controlled, open-label, multicentre superiority trial with sequential design and interim analyses
one_liner: Early decompressive hemicraniectomy in patients ≥61 years with malignant MCA infarction improved 6-month survival without severe disability (mRS 0–4) compared to conservative care, driven by a marked reduction in mortality, though most additional survivors remained substantially dependent.

pico.population: Adults aged ≥61 years with acute malignant MCA infarction (≥2/3 territory involvement, basal ganglia affected, NIHSS ≥20 dominant hemisphere or ≥15 non-dominant, and depressed consciousness)
pico.intervention: Early decompressive hemicraniectomy (large fronto-temporo-parietal craniectomy ≥12 cm diameter, dural opening, duraplasty) plus maximum conservative ICU care, within 48 hours of symptom onset
pico.comparison: Maximum conservative ICU care alone (protocolised neurocritical care) without early decompressive surgery
pico.outcome: Survival without severe disability (mRS 0–4) at 6 months

related_trials: IPD meta-analysis of decompressive hemicraniectomy RCTs

background.existing_knowledge: Malignant MCA infarction causes rapidly progressive cerebral oedema with life-threatening mass effect and historically very high fatality under best medical management. Earlier randomised trials in younger adults showed decompressive hemicraniectomy reduces mortality, but most survivors remain moderately-to-severely disabled.
background.knowledge_gap: Older patients constitute a large proportion of malignant MCA cases but were largely excluded from earlier trials, leaving major uncertainty about the benefit–harm balance, acceptable outcomes, and shared decision-making.
background.hypothesis: Early decompressive hemicraniectomy plus intensive care would increase survival without severe disability (mRS 0–4) at 6 months compared with intensive care alone in patients aged ≥61 years.

methods.design: Prospective, randomised, controlled, open-label, multicentre trial (Germany); 1:1 allocation; sequential triangular design with pre-specified interim analyses and stopping boundary.
methods.setting: Neurocritical care units at participating hospitals.

inclusion: Acute unilateral MCA infarction involving ≥2/3 of the MCA territory (CT or MRI), including basal ganglia
Severe stroke: NIHSS ≥20 if dominant hemisphere; NIHSS ≥15 if non-dominant
Ability to start assigned treatment within 6 hours after randomisation and within 48 hours after symptom onset
exclusion: Contraindication to surgery/anaesthesia or anticipated poor life expectancy due to severe comorbidity
Other causes of impaired consciousness or major competing neurological pathology (e.g., intracranial haemorrhage, tumour)
Known coagulopathy or ongoing anticoagulation not correctable within required timeframe

methods.intervention: Early decompressive hemicraniectomy: large fronto-temporo-parietal craniectomy (typically ≥12 cm diameter), dural opening with duraplasty, bone flap removed for storage and later cranioplasty. Surgery as soon as possible after randomisation (target within 6 hours) and within 48 hours of symptom onset, plus maximum conservative ICU care.
methods.comparison: Maximum conservative ICU care alone, including protocolised neurocritical care (airway/ventilation support as needed, haemodynamic targets, temperature and glucose management, osmotherapy/ICP-directed measures, and management of complications) with no planned hemicraniectomy (rescue surgery allowed only as protocol deviation).
methods.blinding: Open-label treatment; outcome assessors were not part of acute care, but full blinding was not feasible (risk of performance/detection bias).
methods.sample_size_power: Planned maximum 160 patients; sequential triangular design, 90% power to detect an increase in primary endpoint from 8.6% (control) to 31.0% (surgery), two-sided alpha 5%. Trial stopped early for efficacy after 112 patients enrolled (including overrun).
methods.primary_outcome: Survival without severe disability (mRS 0–4) at 6 months.
secondary_outcomes: Health-related quality of life (EQ-5D) at 12 months
Retrospective consent at 12 months (would agree again to assigned treatment)
methods.follow_up: Primary outcome at 6 months (±14 days); key secondary outcomes at 12 months (±14 days).

headline_bullets: Trial stopped early at the first planned interim analysis, after 112 patients randomised.
Primary endpoint (mRS 0–4 at 6 months): 38.5% surgery vs 17.7% control (OR 2.91, 95% CI 1.06 to 7.49, p=0.039; bias‑corrected for sequential monitoring).
Mortality at 6 months fell markedly: 32.7% vs 73.0% (p<0.001).
At 12 months survival remained higher (57.4% vs 24.2%), and mRS 0–4 was 57.4% vs 24.2% (OR 4.42, 95% CI 1.75 to 10.95, p=0.001).
Most surgical survivors had mRS 4 or 5; no patient in either group achieved mRS 0–2 at 6 months.

outcomes_table.outcome: Survival without severe disability (mRS 0–4) at 6 months
outcomes_table.note: Primary analysis, bias‑corrected for sequential monitoring
Secondary endpoint; most survivors still dependent

safety: Total serious adverse events: 88 events in surgery group vs 84 in control group.
Infections and infestations more frequent in surgery group: 18 events vs 8.
Nervous system disorders (including malignant oedema/herniation) more frequent in control group: 23 events vs 46.

domains.notes: Central randomisation stratified by centre; sealed envelopes available as backup. Allocation concealment likely adequate up to assignment. Sequential monitoring increases risk of overestimation; trial used bias‑corrected estimates for primary endpoint.
Open‑label treatment; outcome assessors not part of acute care but full blinding infeasible. Co‑interventions (intensity of supportive care, limitation of therapy) could differ between groups.

Primary endpoint data available for full analysis set at 6 months. At 12 months, outcome denominators reduced (mRS available: 47/49 vs 62/63), introducing potential attrition bias for longer‑term endpoints.

Protocol compliance high: 48/49 (98.0%) received assigned surgery; 62/63 (98.4%) in conservative arm remained without early surgery. Crossovers rare (1 patient in each arm). Per‑protocol primary endpoint OR 3.61 (95% CI 1.20–9.80, p=0.024).
Groups similar in age (median 70 vs 71 years), sex, pre‑stroke function, stroke severity (NIHSS median 18 vs 19), and imaging infarct extent.
Multicentre (Germany) with protocolised surgical standards and ICU care guidance; some variation remain possible.

Randomisation occurred early (median 25 hours from symptom onset in both groups). Time from randomisation to hemicraniectomy was short (median 1.3 hours; IQR 0.7–2.2), supporting biological plausibility for oedema prevention.

Primary endpoint (dichotomised mRS 0–4 vs 5–6) is clinically interpretable but embeds a value judgement about severe disability. Secondary patient‑centred measures (EQ‑5D, HDRS) enrich interpretation.
Sequential design appropriate for high‑mortality condition; early stopping can exaggerate effect sizes and widen confidence intervals. Confidence intervals were wide.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate‑to‑strong: randomisation, high protocol adherence, and strong treatment separation support internal validity, but open‑label design, early stopping, and modest sample size limit certainty about the precise magnitude of benefit and the disability trade‑off.

domains.notes: Enrolled typical malignant MCA phenotype with very severe deficits and low pre‑morbid disability (mRS ≤1). Applies primarily to independent older adults who can undergo major neurosurgery within a narrow time window.

Generalises best to well‑resourced neurocritical care centres with rapid neurosurgical access and rehabilitation. Conducted largely before widespread modern thrombectomy; case‑mix may differ today. Excluded patients with pre‑stroke disability or major comorbidity; extrapolation limited.

external_validity.verdict: Good for independent older adults with true malignant MCA infarction managed in neurocritical care systems capable of rapid surgery; limited for frail patients, delayed presenters, and health systems without consistent neurosurgical capacity.

strengths: Addresses a major evidence gap in older adults, a group under‑represented in earlier decompressive surgery trials.
Clear physiological rationale with tight timing and high protocol adherence; strong separation between strategies.
Patient‑centred secondary outcomes (quality of life, mood) and retrospective consent data enrich clinical interpretation.
Sequential monitoring ethically appropriate for high‑risk surgery with high baseline mortality.
limitations: Open‑label design; potential influence on co‑interventions and treatment limitation decisions.
Early stopping and modest sample size yield wide confidence intervals and potential overestimation of effect.
Primary endpoint uses an arbitrary disability threshold (mRS 0–4) that may not align with all patients’ values, especially with high rates of mRS 4–5 among survivors.
Missing data for some 12‑month outcomes and available‑case analyses for quality‑of‑life measures reduce precision.

critical_appraisal.summary: DESTINY II demonstrates a significant mortality benefit of early decompressive hemicraniectomy in older adults with malignant MCA infarction, but the disability profile among survivors (mostly mRS 4–5) mandates careful shared decision‑making; internal validity is moderate due to open‑label design and early stopping that may inflate the treatment effect.
strengths: Randomised design with high protocol adherence and strong treatment separation.
Patient‑centred outcomes beyond mortality improve clinical interpretation.
weaknesses: Open‑label delivery risks differential care and outcome assessment.
Early stopping produces wide confidence intervals and potential overestimation of effect.
Limited generalisability to patients with pre‑existing disability or delayed presentation.

sections.authors_conclusion: Early decompressive hemicraniectomy in patients ≥61 years with malignant MCA infarction improved survival without severe disability at 6 months, primarily by reducing mortality, with improved quality of life at 12 months; however, most survivors had substantial disability, highlighting the need for thorough counselling.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Early decompressive hemicraniectomy should be offered to appropriately selected older adults (≥61 years, independent pre‑stroke, within 48 hours) after explicit shared decision‑making about the high likelihood of survival with significant dependency (commonly mRS 4–5).
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Patients ≥61 years with acute malignant MCA infarction meeting trial inclusion criteria (severe deficit, large infarct, depressed consciousness) and managed in a centre with rapid neurosurgical access.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: This does not mean that surgery restores independence; most additional survivors will require substantial assistance for daily activities, and many will be severely disabled.
implementation_caveats: Requires a pre‑specified pathway for early recognition and urgent neurosurgical consultation.
The decision must be individualised based on patient/family values regarding acceptable disability.
Generalizability may be limited in low‑resource settings with limited rehabilitation services.

controversies.notes: The pre‑specified primary outcome (mRS 0–4) treats mRS 5 as an unfavourable outcome, yet many surgical survivors were mRS 4–5; the clinical meaning of ‘benefit’ depends on patient values and acceptable dependency levels.
Stopping at an interim analysis can inflate apparent benefit and increase uncertainty around the true treatment effect size, particularly for disability outcomes where confidence intervals were wide.

Differential expectations and treatment limitation practices could influence mortality and disability outcomes in unblinded surgical trials; this remains a critical interpretive lens for any surgery‑versus‑medical management study.

Individual patient data meta‑analysis of randomised trials (including older cohorts) supports a mortality benefit with outcome trade‑offs that vary by age and disability thresholds. European Stroke Organisation and AHA/ASA guidelines recommend decompressive surgery in carefully selected patients, emphasizing time‑sensitivity and shared decision‑making.

context_related_trials.relation: Earlier randomised trials in younger adults showed decompressive hemicraniectomy reduces mortality but with high rates of surviving dependency. DESTINY II extends this evidence to older patients (≥61 years).

context_related_trials.trial: IPD meta‑analysis of decompressive hemicraniectomy RCTs
context_related_trials.relation: Subsequent pooled analysis incorporating DESTINY II confirmed a consistent mortality benefit with age‑dependent disability trade‑offs, reinforcing preference‑sensitive decision‑making.

unresolved_questions: Long‑term functional outcomes beyond 12 months remain uncertain.
Optimal patient selection criteria for surgery in older adults are not fully defined, particularly in the era of reperfusion therapies.
The effect of hemicraniectomy in patients also receiving thrombolysis or thrombectomy needs further study.
Cost‑effectiveness and impact on rehabilitation resource utilisation have not been fully assessed.

numbers_to_remember: Most surgical survivors mRS 4 or 5; no mRS 0–2 at 6 months
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Early hemicraniectomy in older malignant MCA patients substantially lowers mortality but leaves most survivors with substantial dependency—shared decision‑making is fundamental.
